senses: Wearing a cape or capes.
Wearing a cape of a specified kind.
ety: From cape + -ed. Piecewise doublet of capped, chaped, and coped.
examples: One of Batman’s aliases is "the Caped Crusader".
Hella looked about delightedly at all of it, the cafés, the self-contained people, the violent snarl of the traffic, the blue-caped traffic policeman and his white, gleaming club.

senses: An evergreen shrub or small tree, Pistacia lentiscus (mastic tree), native to the Mediterranean.
A hard, brittle, aromatic and transparent resin produced by this tree and used to make varnishes and chewing gum, and as a flavouring.
An alcoholic liquor flavoured with this resin.
ety: From Middle English mastik, from Old French mastic, from Latin mastiche, from Ancient Greek μαστίχη (mastíkhē), from μαστιχάω (mastikháō, “to chew”) (note the chewing gum sense). Related to masticate. The broad sense for cements came via extension from predecessor cements made with the tree's resin. Doublet of mastika.
examples: The mastic, of which the people of Scio gather every year an incredible quantity, is a very rich gum, made use of in medicines, which distils from a shrub called, in Latin, Lentiscus.
Aromatics were used, too, especially in necromancy, and an old recipe of that sort comprises Musk, Myrrh, Frankincense, Red Storax, Mastick, Olibanum, Saffron, Benzoin and Labdanum.

senses: Government by a despot or despots: rule by a singular authority, either a single person or a tight-knit group, which rules with absolute power, especially in a cruel and oppressive way.
ety: From French despotisme; equivalent to despot + -ism.
examples: The iron hand of despotism has quenched the last spark of liberty; hunted down like a wild beast, I am watching an opportunity to fly my degraded and enslaved country.

senses: A person's or a group's conception, philosophy or view of the world; a worldview.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from German Weltanschauung.
examples: Your background and experiences must give you a unique weltanschauung.

senses: Someone who keeps a diary.
ety: From diary + -ist.
examples: Two typical weeks (selected at random and separated by a long interval) are set out in the accompanying tables, and indicate the clear and concise method adopted by the diarist throughout his 42 working years.

senses: An association or institution for the advancement of learning, particularly in science or literature.
The reading room or library of such an association; (by extension) any reading room or library.
A literary or scientific periodical, especially one similar to the London Athenaeum.
ety: From Latin Athenaeum, from Ancient Greek Ᾰ̓θήναιον (Ăthḗnaion), from Ἀθήνη (Athḗnē, “Athene”).
examples: A panel of architects who might loosely be described as the local athenaeum of their profession are awaiting, anxiously, the next edition of the bimonthly journal that bears their names.

senses: The human intestinal parasite Giardia lamblia.
ety: From the genus name Giardia.
examples: As soon as the immune system has generated antibodies against one coat, giardia switches to another.

senses: The spiky edible fruit of this tree, known for its strong taste and very strong, unpleasant odor.
A deep, rich yellow colour, like that of durian flesh (also called durian yellow).
ety: From Malay durian, ultimately from Proto-Austronesian *duʀi (“thorn”). Doublet of iwi, from Māori.
examples: The dessert I thoroughly enjoyed, for the various fruits of Singapore are delicious. One of them, the "durion," exhales a most noxious perfume, but is pleasant to the palate.
Old women crouched over bags of Siamese rice, skeps of red and green peppers, purple egg-plants, bristly rambutans, pineapples, durians.

senses: To thrust oneself in; to come or enter without invitation, permission, or welcome; to encroach; to trespass.
To force in.
ety: From Latin intrudere, from in- + trudere (“to thrust”).
examples: The noise of machinery intruded on an otherwise quiet morning.
Some thoughts rise and intrude upon us, while we shun them; others fly from us, when we would hold them.

senses: A fan, particularly a large fan made of leaf or cloth and hung from the ceiling, (historical) formerly often operated by a servant.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi पंखा (paṅkhā, “fan”), from Sanskrit पक्षक (pakṣaka), from पक्ष (pakṣa, “wing”).
examples: A punkah is, by some, used instead of a chattah, (or umbrella); but it is very inferior as a defence against either sun, wind, or rain.
Outside the court the sun blazed—within was the wind of great punkahs that made you shiver …
In the refreshment room a few would-be passengers were cooled by the punkah, worked by a string tied to the big toe of a sleepy Burmese boy.

senses: The Patriarch, or head of the Abyssinian Church.
ety: From Amharic አቡነ (ʾäbunä), Arabic أَبُونَا (ʔabūnā, “our father”).
examples: Around these leaders are still numerous hereditary dynasties of non-monastic clergy who, over the centuries, might swarm in their thousands to seek ordination on the abun’s rare visits to their area.

senses: Slim but not skinny.
Capable of being easily bent; flexible.
ety: From Middle English lithe, from Old English līþe (“gentle, mild”), from Proto-West Germanic *linþ(ī), from Proto-Germanic *linþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *lentos. Akin to Saterland Frisian lied (“thin, skinny, gaunt”), Danish, Dutch, and archaic German lind (“mild”). Some sources also list Latin lenis (“soft”) and/or Latin lentus (“supple”) as possible cognates.
examples: The coaches are grim, tan, lithe-looking women, clearly twirlers once, on the far side of their glory now and very serious-looking, each with a clipboard and whistle.
Doolittle and myself waited. Colebrook kept on cautiously, squirming his long body in sinuous waves like a lizard's through the grass, and was soon lost to us. No snake could have been lither.

senses: Suggestive of the behaviour of a wasp.
Spiteful or irascible.
ety: From wasp + -ish.
examples: Always, he radiated an air of soigné self-confidence: he could be amiable in his opinions or waspish, but he never betrayed a flicker of doubt about what he thought.

senses: Overly assertive, bold, or determined; aggressively ambitious.
ety: From push + -y.
examples: Pushy parents 'ruin sports days'

senses: Tasting or smelling of garlic.
ety: From garlic + -y.
examples: My companion's Caesar salad, garlickier than most versions, featured homemade croutons.
It opened up a new world of taste and provided me with one of the keenest—and the garlickiest—gastronomic experiences of my life.
Currently, the Palestinian territories are being featured, and the menu boasts treats like maftoul (a garlicky chicken and couscous dish) and tamar Hindi (chilled tamarind juice with rose water).

senses: Bringing about contraction of tissues; harsh, raw, austere.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin stypticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek στυπτικός (stuptikós), from στύφω (stúphō, “to contract”).
examples: Boyles turns to look over his shoulder, squinting into the styptic sun, and then flags a hand over his head.

senses: A process or act of placating; appeasement or an expression of appeasement.
ety: From Latin placatio.
examples: While these political sellout artists have been intoning their mind numbing placations, citizens across the nation have been speaking and acting.

senses: An Indian bread with a texture somewhat resembling puff pastry; sometimes stuffed with vegetables etc.
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani पराठा (parāṭhā) / پَراٹھا (parāṭhā). Doublet of parotta.
examples: In India, shredded radishes are seasoned with chilies, ginger and toasted spices to make a filling for paratha.
Gerry ordered poppadoms and parathas and then he was interrupted by requests for vindaloos, chicken madrases and sag joshes, rice, raita and nan, from Priest, Morgan and Maria Grazia.
It was homemade parathas with keema mattar — ground lamb with peas.

senses: Any of several insects in the superfamily Cicadoidea, with small eyes wide apart on the head and transparent well-veined wings.
The periodical cicada.
ety: Borrowed from Latin cicāda, ultimately onomatopoeic. Doublet of cicala.
examples: Last spring, the periodical cicadas emerged across eastern North America. Their vast numbers and short above-ground life spans inspired awe and irritation in humans—and made for good meals for birds and small mammals.

The emergence years of the principal cicada broods have now been recorded for a long time, and the oldest record of a swarm is that of the appearance of the “locusts” in New England two hundred and ninety-five years ago.

senses: The strip of hardened skin at the base and sides of a fingernail or toenail.
Dead or cornified epidermis.
A thin skin formed on the surface of a liquid.
A protective layer on the shell of a bird's egg.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin cutīcula (“cuticle, skin”). Doublet of cuticula.
examples: By that time she has pushed back his cuticles, cleaned his nails and painted them with clear polish.

senses: Rotting, rotten, being in a state of putrefaction.
Vile, disgusting.
Morally corrupt.
Totally objectionable.
ety: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French putride or directly from Latin putridus (“rotten, decayed”), from putreō (“to be rotten or putrid”), from puter (“rotten, decaying, putrid”).
examples: Quake guzzell dogs, that live on putrid slime.

senses: A drink given to the sick, consisting of ale or wine, bread, and eggs.
ety: Inherited from Middle English caudel, from Old Northern French caudel, from Medieval Latin caldellum, diminutive of Latin caldus, calidus (“warm”).
examples: A venerable lady, known as Great-Aunt Grantley, who had money to bequeath to the Heir, and whom Adrian called The Eighteenth Century, occupied with Hippias the back ground of the house, and shared her caudles with him.

senses: The office of bishop and the governance of a church (a religious denomination) by bishops.
Bishops collectively: Synonym of episcopate.
ety: From episcop (ate) + -acy and/or episcopa(l) + -cy.
examples: Further religious division occurred during the post-Restoration decades in the reign of Charles II, when strenuous and violent efforts were made by the Government to impose an episcopacy on the Scottish Church.

senses: A collaboration, especially a work produced by several musicians who do not usually work together.
ety: Clipping of collaboration. Clipping of collaborate.
examples: UMISEA is a subunit in Hololive featuring idols with nautical themes. The group debuted in 2021 as the first JP+EN collab subunit. Chloe was added to the roster after holox debuted.

senses: A forceful rush or flow forward.
An aggressive assault.
ety: From on- + rush. Compare Middle English onresen (“to rush upon; attack”), from Old English onrǣsan (“to rush, rush on”); Old English onrǣs (“an onrush, assault, attack”).
examples: He caught Grendel's right hand, and still without rising from his bed, stopped the monster's onrush.

senses: A coarse heavy fabric made of jute or hemp.
ety: From Hindi and Marathi गनी (ganī) or गोन (gon), from Sanskrit गोणी (goṇī), ultimately of Dravidian origin. Doublet of gunia.
examples: Traffic is brisk, and goods consists of rice, gunny (hessian), maize and native implements.
Provisions were ferried by camel in stout sacks of gunny with blocks of ice packed round them; a herculean task.

senses: A certain breed of dog having short legs and a long trunk, including standard-sized, miniature (smooth-haired, long-haired, and short-haired) varieties.
ety: From German Dachshund (literally “badger dog”), from German Dachs (“badger”) + Hund (“dog”).
examples: Say what you will of dachshunds, their peculiar shape makes them the easiest breed of dog to trip over in existence.
We had decided to take a small dog for the children and we chose a tan, short-haired, six-week-old male dachshund. We named him Fritz.

senses: Sweet; nice; pleasant.
ety: From Middle English douce, from Old French dolz, dous, Middle French doux, douce, from Latin dulcis (“sweet”). Doublet of dolce, doux, and dulce.
examples: Beyond the bed stood the woman. Dark and pale, aged about twenty-one . . . his mother, Mary de Bohun. Death had stolen none of her douce beauty and sweetness.
The sun broke through the cloods, and the douce song o’ a laverock filled me wi’ gledness.

senses: A hypothetical device capable of inducing orgasm.
ety: From orgasm + -tron, introduced in the film Sleeper (1973).
examples: We do not know of any real-life orgasmatrons, even vibrators.

senses: Synonym of ornithopter (“birdlike aircraft”).
ety: Clipping of ornithopter.
examples: Another ’thopter glided in over the cliff wall above Hawat. He drew in a sharp breath as he saw it—a big troop-carrier. It flew with the slow, spread-wing heaviness of a full load like a giant bird coming to its nest.
I'm sending down five more dropships, combat EMVs, and a thopter gunship.
Flowstone Thopter gets +1/-1 and gains flying until end of turn.

senses: The action of destroying or ruining; destruction, ruin.
ety: From Late Middle English spoliacioun (“looting, robbery, theft; an instance of this; (ecclesiastical) wrongful deprivation of the emoluments of a benefice due to another”), from Anglo-Norman spoliacioun, espolïacion, and directly from their etymon Latin spoliātiō (“plundering, robbing”), from spoliāre + -tiō (suffix forming nouns denoting a process, action, or result of an action). Spoliāre is the present active infinitive of spoliō (“to deprive or strip of clothing or covering, unclothe, uncover; (by extension) to pillage, plunder; etc.”), from spolium (“hide or skin stripped off an animal; (
examples: There is much sad evidence, too, of the spoliation and dereliction of vanished industry: tips, slag-heaps and derelict colliery-screens among which the ubiquitous, nomad mountain sheep graze unconcernedly.

senses: The offering of worship, thanks etc. to a deity.
A deed or gift offered charitably.
ety: From Middle English oblacioun, from Old French oblacion, from Latin oblātiō (“offering”), from offerō (“to offer, present”). By surface analysis, oblate + -ion.
examples: As she waits for her children in the shade / Demogorgon or demigod the ghost parade / No oblation will bring her back to our place

senses: Life force, according to Maori beliefs.
ety: Borrowed from Māori mauri.
examples: We're just cuzzies from down at the marae down the road that are trying to be proactive and look after our whenua, look after our stories, and look after the mauri of our awa, our river.

senses: Containing fewer allergens; minimally allergenic.
ety: Coined between 1950 and 1955 from hypo- + allergenic. Some say that it was coined by advertisers in 1953. Merriam-Webster puts the date at 1940.
examples: However, unless you have a nonshedding, nonlicking breed, there's no such thing as a truly hypoallergenic dog. How about a nice goldfish instead?

senses: Marriage; the state of being married.
The ceremony of marriage.
A particular solitaire card game using two decks of cards.
ety: From Old French matremoine, from Latin mātrimōnium (“marriage, wedlock”), from mātri(s) (“mother”) + -mōnium (“obligation”). By surface analysis, matri- + -mony. Compare patrimony.
examples: If either of you know any impediment, why ye may not be lawfully joined together in matrimony, ye do now confess it.

senses: A slaughterhouse or abattoir.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish matadero.
examples: In connection with one of these markets a matadero has been built, in the form of a detached building.

senses: A male ballet dancer.
ety: Borrowed from Italian ballerino.
examples: BALLERINOS WANTED / Can use a few trained ballerinos for "Song of Norway" tour. Auditions TODAY at 2 p.m., Masonic Temple, Hollywood. Bring practice clothes and toe shoes.
As aware as you are, though, consider how much more keenly the leaping ballerinas and ballerinos of the world feel the tow with every move they make.

senses: To illegally take possession of (something, especially items of low value); to pilfer, to steal.
ety: From Middle English filchen (“to pilfer, steal”). The further origin of the word is uncertain, but it is likely from or related to Old English fylċian (“to marshal troops”) and Old English ġefylċe (“band of men, army, host”), which would make it also related to folk.
examples: Hey, someone filched my wallet!
The farm drivers were often found to be filching from the cars for spare parts or moonlighting with trucks for personal gain.

senses: A medieval primitive cannon, used chiefly in sieges for throwing heavy stone balls.
A bombardon.
ety: From Middle English bombard, from Middle French bombarde (“a bombard, mortar, catapult"; also "a bassoon-like musical instrument”), from Latin bombus (“buzzing; booming”). The modern pronunciation is from modern French bombarde.
examples: They planted in divers places twelve great bombards, wherewith they threw huge stones into the air, which, falling down into the city, might break down the houses.

senses: Having a delayed response to a change in the factors influencing it.
ety: From lag + -y.
examples: Gasoline prices usually show a laggier response to crude-oil price reduction than to crude-oil price increases.
